newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: West wins on landmines at UN after Syria steps out.
newsitem.headline: West wins on landmines at UN after Syria steps out.

text.p: The West won a decision on Thursday to appoint a special coordinator who will try to launch negotiations on a global landmines ban at the Conference on Disarmament .
The decision was possible after Syria's delegate left the conference room to pave the way for consensus at the United Nations-sponsored forum, according to diplomats.
The United States and Britain welcomed the breakthrough, while non-aligned countries including India and Cuba said the precedent was dangerous.

"My delegation and government welcome the decision to appoint a special coordintor to conduct consultations on a possible mandate on the question of landmines," Katharine Crittenberger, acting head of the U.S. delegation, said.
The move should help the forum decide its contribution to "stemming the weapons' catastrophic consequences for civilian populations", she added.
Crittenberger said that Washington hoped the special coordinator could be named soon and make a quick report which would lead to setting up a formal negotiating committee.
The decision came a day before the Geneva body ends its second session of 1997 and begins a summer recess before opening its final seven-week session of the year on July 28.

Maria Krasnohorska, the Slovakian ambassador who currently serves as chairwoman, asked the 61 member states to say whether they could accept a draft Western text put forward last week by Australia which proposed naming a special coordinator on mines.
Seeing no objection, she announced: "It is so decided."

Western diplomats had feared Syria and Cuba might hold up consensus on naming a special coordinator to seek consensus on talks on banning the use, storage, production and transfer of landmines. The arms are blamed for causing 25,000 deaths a year.
But Syria's delegate left the room before the question was put -- a neat way of avoiding a fatal veto, diplomats said.

This could have called into question a tricky compromise decision adopted a year ago under which Syria and 22 other states were admitted to the U.N. arms forum on condition they not individually veto decisions during the first two years.
India's ambassador Arundhati Ghose, in brief remarks, said: "We have no problem with the (landmines) decision.
"But we are very concerned that one delegation had to absent itself (leave the room) in order to see that the CD can take a decision," she added. "I hope it is not a precedent."

The Geneva talks had been deadlocked all year due to a row between Western states eager to negotiate global bans on landmines and production of bomb-making fissile material, and non-aligned states seeking greater elimination of nuclear arms.
Ghose, a major voice among the some 30 non-aligned countries who belong to the Geneva talks, said: "In our view, consensus is there to protect the weak -- not to ignore the weak.
"It is true that we are not important. But we expect to be treated as equals and we expect that our priorities will be given consideration and a response."
Ghose said: "I don't believe that the appointment of a special coordinator has in any way solved any problems which genuinely exist at the CD."
Cuba's envoy Carlos Amat Fores took the floor to say: "We have the same malaise as the Ambassador of India.
"My delegation considers we must immediately reach agreement on a programme of work."
"The decision adopted (on landmines) is selective and distant from the priority objectives of the CD," he added.
Earlier, China's ambassador Sha Zukang made a speech arguing in favour of negotiating a landmines ban in phases, but said he would not object to naming a special coordinator on the issue.

The weapons remained an "indispensable, legitimate and conventional means of national defense" for his vast country which has long land borders and an "uncertain security environment", according to Beijing's envoy.
"China is in favour of imposing strict and feasible restrictions on anti-personnel landmines and their use, thereby achieving the objective of an ultimate ban in a step-by-step manner," Sha said.
"In short, China is not opposed to the objective of (the) prohibition of anti-personnel landmines realised in a phased approach, but cannot agree to any immediate total ban," he said.
